content: These are Excel/Google-Sheets dynamic-array reshape and construction functions (HSTACK, VSTACK, SORT, TOCOL, TOROW, WRAPCOLS, WRAPROWS, plus the inline-array form of FREQUENCY). Excel, Google Sheets, Lattice, and the `formulas` npm library all implement them and agree on the spilled result up to shape. HyperFormula, IronCalc, and pycel do not implement any of these names and therefore return #NAME? (unrecognized-name). Confirmed live: HyperFormula and IronCalc return #NAME? for every one of these, and pycel returns #NAME? as well. The libreoffice branch here is a recording artifact, not a genuine result — see the INDEX annotation: the whole arrays/array-longtail libreoffice fixture (generated 2026-05-11) came back blank even for functions LibreOffice has supported for decades, so its [[blank]] value should not be read as LibreOffice behavior.

_meta.evidence: recorded fixtures + live probe (hyperformula/ironcalc/pycel all #NAME?; formulas returns the spilled array)

content: SEQUENCE is supported by Excel, Google Sheets, and Lattice, which spill the requested grid of sequential numbers. It is NOT implemented by the `formulas` npm library, HyperFormula, IronCalc, or pycel, all four of which return #NAME?. This distinguishes SEQUENCE from the sibling stack/reshape functions in the same suite (HSTACK, VSTACK, SORT, TOCOL...), where `formulas` DOES implement the function — so `formulas` sits in the supported branch there but in the #NAME? branch here. Confirmed live: `formulas` returns #NAME? for SEQUENCE(2,3), SEQUENCE(3), and SEQUENCE(1). The libreoffice [[blank]] is a whole-suite recording artifact (see INDEX annotation).

_meta.evidence: recorded fixtures + live probe (formulas/hyperformula/ironcalc/pycel all return #NAME? for SEQUENCE)

content: FLATTEN is a Google-Sheets-proprietary function (it collapses one or more ranges into a single column in row-major order) and has never been added to Excel's function set. Only Google Sheets and Lattice implement it and return the flattened column. Excel, the `formulas` library, HyperFormula, IronCalc, and pycel all lack the name and return #NAME?. Confirmed live: `formulas`, HyperFormula, IronCalc, and pycel each return #NAME? for FLATTEN({1,2;3,4}). Because Excel itself does not have FLATTEN, this is not merely an incomplete open-source engine gap — a workbook using FLATTEN is not portable to Excel at all. The libreoffice [[blank]] is a recording artifact (see INDEX annotation).

_meta.evidence: recorded fixtures + live probe (formulas/hyperformula/ironcalc/pycel #NAME?); FLATTEN is documented as Google Sheets only

content: INDEX(A1:B2, 2, 1) evaluates to 20 in all seven engines that produced a real result — Excel, Google Sheets, HyperFormula, IronCalc, Lattice, pycel, and the `formulas` library — confirmed live for HyperFormula, IronCalc, pycel, and formulas. The only divergent branch is libreoffice, which recorded [[blank]]. INDEX is one of the oldest spreadsheet functions and is fully supported by LibreOffice Calc, so a blank result is impossible as genuine behavior. This is the tell that the entire arrays and array-longtail libreoffice fixture (platform `libreoffice`, generatedAt 2026-05-11) is a systematic capture failure: every case in these two suites recorded [[blank]] regardless of function, including universally-supported ones like INDEX. The libreoffice branch across this whole batch should be treated as missing data, not as a divergence, and the suites re-recorded on LibreOffice.

_meta.evidence: recorded fixtures (libreoffice=blank for INDEX, which it supports) + live probe (all 4 pure engines = 20); artifact spans the whole suite

content: MINVERSE({1,2;2,4}) inverts a singular matrix (determinant 0), so the engines that implement MINVERSE correctly refuse: Excel, Google Sheets, Lattice, and the `formulas` library all return #NUM!. Confirmed live that `formulas` returns #NUM!. HyperFormula, IronCalc, and pycel instead return #NAME? — but for a different reason: they do not implement MINVERSE at all (confirmed live), so they never reach the singularity check. The two error branches thus have unrelated causes: #NUM! is a genuine numeric-domain refusal, while #NAME? is an unimplemented-name error. (Note: MINVERSE's ordinary non-singular cases for hyperformula/ironcalc/pycel are already covered by DV-0003; this singular-matrix case is the uncovered fork.) The libreoffice [[blank]] is a recording artifact (see INDEX annotation).

LOGEST (exponential-regression coefficients) and the exponential-projection form of GROWTH are implemented by Excel, Google Sheets, Lattice, and the `formulas` library, which agree up to floating-point precision (the multiple value sub-groups in the supported partition class differ only in the last few ULPs, e.g. GROWTH's 31.999999999999993 vs 31.99999999999998). HyperFormula, IronCalc, and pycel do not implement LOGEST or GROWTH and return #NAME? — confirmed live for all three. This is a clean missing-function split; unlike LINEST/TREND, pycel offers no partial implementation of LOGEST or GROWTH. The libreoffice [[blank]] is a recording artifact (see INDEX annotation).

_meta.evidence: recorded fixtures + live probe (hyperformula/ironcalc/pycel #NAME? for LOGEST and GROWTH)

content: These are the stats-table forms of LINEST and LOGEST (4th argument TRUE requests the full regression-statistics block, spilling 5 rows by N columns). Excel, Google Sheets, and the `formulas` library all produce the 5-row block but disagree in cells that are mathematically degenerate for a perfect-fit line: the F-statistic / degrees-of-freedom cell is #NUM! in Excel but a finite very-large number in Google Sheets and formulas (e.g. Excel returns #NUM! where gsheets returns ~2.25e31 and formulas ~2.80e30), and the standard-error cells that should be 0 come out as different tiny non-zero floats per engine — this is a precision/degenerate-case divergence within the supported engines. Lattice implements plain LINEST/LOGEST but NOT the stats form, so it returns #N/A (a missing argument-form). HyperFormula and IronCalc return #NAME? (function absent). For LINEST/linest-with-stats pycel returns a single scalar (see the LINEST-coefficient annotation), while for LOGEST/logest-with-stats pycel returns #NAME? (LOGEST absent). The libreoffice [[blank]] is a recording artifact (see INDEX annotation).

_meta.evidence: recorded fixtures (lattice #N/A on stats form; excel #NUM! vs gsheets/formulas huge-number in the F-stat cell) + live probe (formulas full block; hyperformula/ironcalc #NAME?)

content: LINEST({y},{x}) and LINEST({y}) (no stats) return the [slope, intercept] coefficient pair. Excel, Google Sheets, Lattice, and the `formulas` library all return the 1-row-by-2-column pair and agree up to floating-point precision. HyperFormula and IronCalc do not implement LINEST and return #NAME?. pycel implements LINEST but does not spill the full coefficient array — it returns only the first element (the slope) as a single scalar (confirmed live: LINEST({1,2,3},{1,2,3}) -> 1.0000000000000002; LINEST({2,4,6,8}) -> 1.9999999999999993), dropping the intercept. That scalar-collapse is an array-handling limitation, not a wrong number. The libreoffice [[blank]] is a recording artifact (see INDEX annotation).

_meta.evidence: recorded fixtures + live probe (pycel returns a lone scalar slope; hyperformula/ironcalc #NAME?)

content: TREND (linear least-squares fitted / projected values) splits several ways among the engines that implement it. Excel, Google Sheets, and Lattice agree (up to precision) and spill the result in the natural orientation of the requested points. The `formulas` library returns the values in a transposed orientation for the inferred-x and simple cases — TREND({2,4,6,8}) comes back as a 4x1 COLUMN in formulas versus a 1x4 ROW in Excel/gsheets, and TREND({1,2,3},{1,2,3},{4,5}) as a 2x1 column versus a 1x2 row — an array-orientation divergence. When new_x is supplied as a separate array whose orientation differs from x (TREND/trend-new-x, {5;6;7}), `formulas` cannot reconcile the shapes and returns #REF! (confirmed live). pycel implements TREND but collapses the spill to a single scalar (first fitted value only; confirmed live). HyperFormula and IronCalc do not implement TREND and return #NAME?. The libreoffice [[blank]] is a recording artifact (see INDEX annotation).

_meta.evidence: recorded fixtures + live probe (formulas transposes inferred-x to a column and returns #REF! on separate new_x; pycel returns a scalar; hyperformula/ironcalc #NAME?)

content: GROWTH's inferred-x and new-x forms mirror the TREND divergences among the implementing engines. Excel, Google Sheets, and Lattice agree up to precision and spill in the natural orientation. The `formulas` library returns GROWTH({2,4,8,16}) transposed to a 4x1 column rather than the 1x4 row Excel/gsheets produce (array-orientation), and returns #REF! for GROWTH({2,4,8,16},{1,2,3,4},{5;6}) where new_x is a separate array with a differing orientation (confirmed live). Unlike TREND/LINEST, pycel does NOT implement GROWTH and returns #NAME? here (along with HyperFormula and IronCalc). The libreoffice [[blank]] is a recording artifact (see INDEX annotation).

_meta.evidence: recorded fixtures + live probe (formulas transposes inferred-x, #REF! on separate new_x; hyperformula/ironcalc/pycel #NAME?)
